overview.title: Loading Xception and building a feature extractor
overview.main_topic: Instantiating the ImageNet-pretrained Xception backbone and its preprocessor with KerasHub, listing its convolutional layers, and building a single-output feature-extractor model for layer block3_sepconv1
overview.central_idea: To visualize filters, you need a model that maps an input image to the activation of one chosen convolutional layer. Because the KerasHub Xception backbone is a functional model, you can look up any layer by name with `get_layer` and wrap `model.input` → `layer.output` in a new `keras.Model`, with no need to rewrite Xception.
overview.importance: The feature extractor is the differentiable function whose output the gradient-ascent loop will maximize. The pattern of building a sub-model from inspectable functional layers is reused for Grad-CAM in section 10.3.
learning_objectives: Load a pretrained backbone and its matching ImageConverter with `from_preset`
List a model's Conv2D and SeparableConv2D layers with `isinstance`
Build a feature extractor from `model.input` and `layer.output`
Explain why functional models are inspectable
prerequisites: KerasHub backbones and the `xception_41_imagenet` preset (section 8.3, p.282–283)
Functional API and multi-output models; listing 10.3 (p.311)

summary:
The page completes the sentence from p.315: filter visualization will be the reader's second example of a low-level gradient descent loop (the first was in chapter 2), and it will be shown for **TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX**.

**Listing 10.7** instantiates the ImageNet-trained Xception model with KerasHub, "exactly as we did in chapter 8". `keras_hub.models.Backbone.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet")` builds the feature-extractor network from pretrained weights. `keras_hub.layers.ImageConverter.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet", image_size=(180, 180))` loads the matching preprocessing that scales input images. (In KerasHub a *backbone* is the network without its classification head, p.282.)

The convolutional layers of interest are the `Conv2D` and `SeparableConv2D` layers, and their names are needed to retrieve their outputs. **Listing 10.8** prints those names in depth order by looping over `model.layers` and filtering with `isinstance`. The `SeparableConv2D` layers have names like `block6_sepconv1` and `block7_sepconv2`, because **Xception is structured into blocks**, each containing several convolutional layers.

Next comes a second model, a **feature extractor**, that returns the output of one specific layer. Because the backbone is a **Functional API model, it is inspectable**: you can query a layer's `output` and reuse it in a new model, with no need to copy the entire Xception code. **Listing 10.9** picks `layer_name = "block3_sepconv1"` (any layer of the convolutional base could be used instead), fetches the layer object with `model.get_layer(name=layer_name)`, and builds `feature_extractor = keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer.output)`. Given an input image, this model returns the output of the target layer.

The next page (p.317) applies the feature extractor with the model-specific preprocessing and defines the loss to maximize.

paragraphs.what_it_means: Filter visualization targets the filters of convolution layers. Listing 10.8 iterates over `model.layers`, which for a functional model are stored in topological (depth) order, and prints the names that pass the `isinstance` filter.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The SeparableConv2D layers have names like `block6_sepconv1` and `block7_sepconv2`, because Xception is organized into blocks, each containing several convolutional layers.

paragraphs.what_it_says: A second model, a 'feature extractor', will return the output of one specific layer. Because the backbone is a functional model it is inspectable: you can query any layer's `output` and reuse it in a new model without copying Xception's code.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A functional model keeps its graph of layers and symbolic tensors. `layer.output` is the symbolic tensor flowing out of that layer when the model's input flows in, so `keras.Model(model.input, layer.output)` defines the sub-graph from the input to that layer. It shares the pretrained weights and simply stops at the chosen layer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is what makes the gradient-ascent loss computable: the loss is a function of `feature_extractor(image)`, and the gradient flows back through the shared layers to the image.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Unlike the nine-output model of listing 10.3, this one has a single output; the same mechanism is used again for Grad-CAM (p.325).

concepts.name: KerasHub backbone and preset
concepts.definition: A pretrained feature-extractor network without its classification head, loaded with `Backbone.from_preset(name)`, which downloads configuration and weights.
concepts.intuition: A ready-made convolutional base, fetched by name.
concepts.technical: `keras_hub.models.Backbone.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet")`; the matching `ImageConverter.from_preset(...)` reproduces the pretraining image scaling.
concepts.significance: Supplies the pretrained Xception whose filters are visualized.
concepts.misconception: The backbone does not output ImageNet class probabilities; that requires a KerasHub task model (used for Grad-CAM, p.324).

concepts.name: Feature extractor sub-model
concepts.definition: A Keras model built from an existing model's input and one intermediate layer's output.
concepts.intuition: Tapping the network at a chosen depth.
concepts.technical: `keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=model.get_layer(name).output)`; shares weights with the parent.
concepts.significance: Provides the activation that gradient ascent will maximize.
concepts.misconception: It is not a copy, so modifying the weights of one would change the other.

concepts.name: Inspectability of functional models
concepts.definition: Functional models expose their layers and the symbolic input/output tensors of each, so sub-graphs can be reused as new models.
concepts.intuition: The model is a map you can read, not a sealed box.
concepts.significance: The page notes there is no need to copy the entire Xception code.
concepts.misconception: Subclassed models do not generally offer the same `layer.output` graph access.

concepts.name: SeparableConv2D
concepts.definition: A convolution factorized into a depthwise spatial convolution and a pointwise 1 × 1 convolution.
concepts.intuition: Look at spatial patterns per channel first, then mix channels.
concepts.technical: Fewer parameters and computations than Conv2D for the same output depth; the main layer type in Xception.
concepts.significance: Most layers listed by listing 10.8 are of this type, named blockN_sepconvM.
concepts.misconception: SeparableConv2D is not a subclass of Conv2D in Keras, which is why both classes are listed in the isinstance tuple.

code.title: Instantiating the Xception convolutional base
code.original_code:
import keras_hub

model = keras_hub.models.Backbone.from_preset(
    "xception_41_imagenet",
)
preprocessor = keras_hub.layers.ImageConverter.from_preset(
    "xception_41_imagenet",
    image_size=(180, 180),
)

deeper.title: Why three backends?
deeper.body: Note (not in the book's text on this page): the feature extractor is a Keras model and runs on any backend, but computing a gradient with respect to the *input image* uses each framework's own autodiff API. TensorFlow records operations with `tf.GradientTape` and calls `tape.gradient`. PyTorch marks the image tensor with `requires_grad` and calls `.backward()`. JAX uses `jax.grad` of a pure function, which requires the model's stateless call. Sections 10.2.1–10.2.3 (p.318–319) give these versions.

deeper.title: Reading a layer name
deeper.body:
`block3_sepconv1`:
1. `block3` is the third block of the network, early in the hierarchy.
2. `sepconv` means a SeparableConv2D layer.
3. `1` is the first such layer in that block.
The layers from early blocks are expected to show simpler patterns than those from deep blocks such as `block8_sepconv1` (see p.322).

deeper.title: A tap on a pipe
deeper.body: The backbone is a long water pipe of filters. `get_layer(...).output` drills a tap at one point, and `keras.Model(model.input, tap)` is a short pipe that ends at that tap. Water (gradients) can still flow backward from the tap to the inlet.

takeaways: Filter visualization uses a hand-written gradient loop, the book's second after chapter 2, shown for TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.
Listing 10.7 loads the Xception backbone and its matching preprocessor via KerasHub presets.
Listing 10.8 prints Conv2D/SeparableConv2D layer names; Xception names them by block (blockN_sepconvM).
Listing 10.9 builds a feature extractor from `model.input` to `get_layer("block3_sepconv1").output`.
This works because functional models are inspectable; no Xception code needs to be copied.

questions.question: What does `keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer.output)` produce in listing 10.9?
options: A copy of Xception with new random weights
A model that, given an input image, returns the output of the target layer, sharing Xception's weights
A classifier that predicts ImageNet classes
A model that returns the filter weights of the layer
questions.answer: A model that, given an input image, returns the output of the target layer, sharing Xception's weights
questions.explanation: The callout states this. Weights are reused, not re-initialized, no classification head is involved, and the output is an activation, not kernel weights.

questions.question: Why must listing 10.8 test for both `Conv2D` and `SeparableConv2D`?
questions.answer: Because Xception contains both kinds of convolution layers, and the authors are interested in all of them; SeparableConv2D is a separate class, so testing only Conv2D would miss most of Xception's layers.
questions.explanation: The page names both types as the convolutional layers of interest.

questions.question: What property of the model makes listing 10.9 possible, and why does that save work?
questions.answer: It is a Functional API model and therefore inspectable: you can query a layer's output and reuse it in a new model, so there's no need to copy the entire Xception code.

questions.question: What does the name `block7_sepconv2` tell you about a layer?
questions.answer: It is the second SeparableConv2D layer in block 7 of Xception.
questions.explanation: Xception is structured into blocks each containing several convolutional layers, and names follow that structure.

questions.question: What is the role of the `preprocessor` created in listing 10.7?
options: It augments images with random flips
It scales (and resizes) input images to match Xception's pretraining preprocessing
It converts class indices into labels
questions.answer: It scales (and resizes) input images to match Xception's pretraining preprocessing
questions.explanation: The callout says it loads the matching preprocessing to scale input images; p.317 stresses scaling to the same range as the pretraining data. It does no augmentation, label decoding or freezing.

questions.question: How does listing 10.9 differ from listing 10.3's activation model, and why is a single output enough here?
questions.answer: Listing 10.3 had nine outputs, one per Conv/Pool layer, to visualize all activations. Here only one layer's filters are being visualized at a time, so the feature extractor needs only that layer's output.
questions.explanation: Both use model.input and layer outputs; the purpose differs.

questions.question: Could you change listing 10.9 to target a deeper layer, and predict how its filter visualizations would differ from those of block3_sepconv1?
questions.answer: Replace layer_name with e.g. "block8_sepconv1"; deeper filters should show more complex, textured patterns.
